reviews.text: Okay, let me get some important info out the way first: 1. I am a kickstarter backer, if you feel that makes me have potential bias then I understand, and 2. My review of this game comes not necessarily from the version available right now, but across a longer period of time, over multiple versions that were however feature complete so not radically different to this early access release version. Okay, got that...alright here we go: I love Timemelters, I think it's charming, clever, unique and honestly kind of brilliant. Okay so what is it? Well in essence it's a strategy...puzzle.....spellslinging.......?????? game?! Okay it is a game, that's for sure. Basically you run around and cast spells to stop evil things, these spells use resources so you need to be clever about their use....and then you time travel and continue to do that alongside a recording of you, trying not to interrupt the timeline in the process...and then you start incorporating increasingly bizarre and clever time-travel strategies involving teleportation, farming resources for future timelines to collect, and performing feats like killing a boss by attacking 4 versions of itself AT THE SAME TIME. What Timemelters revels in is the satisfaction of a clever plan coming together, of going for an idea, for a strategy, and performing a piece of it one bit at a time to make an overall master-plan happen. you can pause at any time to overview the battlefield and the order of events you have created, it's all introduced gradually, and at least for me (everyone experiences difficulties differently so take this with a grain of salt) it's so far always remained at that right balance of satisfying challenge, without being hopelessly overwhelming, it's full of "Aha" moments and clutch situations and just a whole lot of heart; it's one of those games you can feel the "soul" of a bit and I am very susceptible to that kind of thing xD Now I will say that it's not without its shortcomings; while I think the story has some interesting moments it's not always the most exciting thing in the world and its delivery can feel a bit stilted, and whenever I open the game the main characters eyes stare into my soul and it terrifies me....It's not a game they're going to show at nvidia conventions to brag about graphics but, I will say, it actually is full of interesting teleports and cool effects that do make it stand out but....yh Teagan's death stare will forever haunt my dreams so just know that she will haunt yours too; on the upside though the soundtrack does have some great tracks on it, you'll become quite familiar with them but there's a few that when they come on always get me cheering and humming along so that's always fun :) Beyond just the campaign you've also got the challenge puzzles which subvert initial solutions in weird ways and, yh, do you get it yet? I like the game xD Honestly for the price I think it's a bit of a bargain so, go, now, stop reading this and get it (financial situation allowing of course)!

[quote] Timemelters is a really creative blend of genres that results in hours of fun both actively fighting enemies and testing your brain by strategizing, preparing the terrain and sequence of events around you to ensure your victory. If you’re into strategy titles, this is a must! [/quote] In the steam reviews for the game, I see a lot of different attempts at defining its genre. I see people calling it a [b]tower defense game, I saw action RPG, there were lots of mentions of strategy, I’ve seen it being called a puzzle game… surprisingly enough, these are all correct![/b] It all boils down to the central mechanic of rewinding time. [b]The gameplay basically works like this: in every mission, you have a central objective. Sometimes you have to protect someone, other times you have to kill all the enemies… It varies.[/b] In the stages, you get multiple waves of enemies, often coming from different but predetermined paths, as seen on the picture below. Usually, they all head to the same place (most often, that’s you or whoever you’re trying to protect). If a single enemy hits you, that’s it, you’re dead and must start over (exceptions apply, they’ll be explained shortly). To accomplish your goal, you can [b] trigger traps on the path of the enemies, change their paths altogether, place sentries (that also die in 1 hit) to hit them and get their attention, amongst many other options.[/b] And as another resource, you also have… yourself. [b]Many times you will be in the fray, using bolts of light to pick off enemies[/b] - just be careful as you can easily get swarmed and die!... Well, kinda. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2875651317 This “kinda” is where the time manipulation mechanic comes into play. At any given point of your choosing, or instantly upon being hit, time rewinds (depending on the level - some levels take that mechanic away from you) and you’re thrust back into the start of the combat. Except this time, you’re helped by none other than your past self! Every time you rewind, you create an Echo. [b]That means your previous attempts get replayed in real time, as you try again. If you stay still in your new life, events will play out exactly as they did before you first died.[/b] But where’s the fun in staying still? [b]While your Echo triggers the same traps you did on your first go, and gets rid of the same enemies you did on your first attempt, your second (or third or fourth…) life is now free to go do something else.[/b] And this cycle keeps going until you run out of Echoes you can create. This is why the game is a mix of genres: you do end up defending your position from enemies following a set path, which is often seen on tower defense games. You hop into the fray actively combating enemies, on a basic action system. And at the very same time, you also coordinate a strategy that makes use of your multiple lives, echoes, traps and skills to make sure you win the map. [b]The map design is solid, and some very interesting scenarios are created in them.[/b] Just don’t go in expecting an open world grand adventure - this isn’t it. The maps are all linear (much like in tower defense games), with a clear objective in mind. This works in the game’s favour, though, as it allows for better scenarios to be crafted and for the player to better control the outcome of the battle. And if you, like me, end up really enjoying the combat, I have good news: [b]the game has 40 challenge scenarios that you can tackle![/b] These limit your skills and can have unique spawn, enemy placements and goals for you to accomplish. Some of them get really challenging from what I’ve seen. [b]The story can also be played on multiple difficulty settings, though I don’t know if it’s enough to warrant replaying the entire campaign multiple times.[/b] I played through it on “Balanced”, which is basically the game’s normal mode. True to its name, the experience felt tough at times, but never TOO tough. And if you do get stuck, the game does offer a button that gives you tips for each stage. Personally, I feel some of those tips went a bit too far, being more so instructions to win rather than hints, but regardless, I know this is what some people would prefer - it’s personal preference. The combat can also be slightly customized via the use of perks. You have the option to unlock around 1/4th of the total amount of perks throughout the story. Choose wisely, as I don’t think you can change your choice, unfortunately. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2875650904 Another factor I’d like to highlight is the story. The devs crafted a fantastic world here! [b]The lore they created, while not explored too deeply, is fascinating, and the story they chose to tell with it had me hooked from beginning to end.[/b] I may be biased as I’m a sucker for time travel elements in storylines, but still, it was solid, and I can’t wait to see more from the devs. The steam store page doesn’t say much, so I’ll refrain from doing so as well. Just know that it involves witches, time travel, chaos and even a couple of plot twists. [b]The graphics in the game are admittedly (by the devs themselves) not the best, but that’s really not an issue at all.[/b] The artstyle inside some cutscenes though is incredibly nice, as you can see in one of the pictures in this review! The soundtrack also perfectly complements the mood the game is going for at any given moment. The game also has voice acting! Well, at least during the special cutscenes with the artstyle mentioned above. The rest of the game only has a few voiced lines, unfortunately. [b]While I did gush over the game a lot, it’s not without its issues.[/b] Aside from what I’ve already mentioned, the game could also do with a way to replay story levels (if there are any, I haven’t found them) and small improvements such as a menu between missions or something to allow for an easy quit point, change your perk choices, etc. It’s also sometimes tough to predict what will happen during missions. I’ve died more than a few times trying to understand things such as enemy waves’ attack patterns (who they prioritized, why some of them went for my bait while others continued moving, etc), and this sort of trial and error can be annoying to some. I did also run into a few (8 or so) issues. Most of them were very, VERY minor things such as a random house I could walk through or a typo, but a couple of them did soft lock me and force me to reload my checkpoint. Even on those, though, I only lost 2 minutes of gameplay. I’m honestly not worried about these issues as I’ve sent evidence of all of them to the devs, which have been very responsive. Plus, 8 or so issues in 8 or so hours of gameplay means the game is already pretty polished, especially given that it’s in early access. So yeah, I’m fully confident most if not all will be fixed by the time the game fully releases. And speaking of early access: the main story and challenges are all here. In fact, most of the game is. [b]All in all, this is a really solid and unique game. Oh, and did I mention it has co-op?[/b] You can play the entire campaign with a friend (albeit only online, no split-screen). I couldn’t test it as that requires, well, having friends, but people have been saying it works well! If any of this seems interesting to you, I urge you to give Timemelters a shot!

So this is complicated. I've totally rewritten big chunks of this review, because my opinion changed. Still thumbs up, but not as enthusiastically up as it was before. You ever played the story mode of any of the RTSes of yore? Like, say, Supreme Commander? Beating the maps was kind of a "puzzle", only in that you wound up having to try the maps several times, trying different tactics each time, putting a different turret over here, or building up over there, and exactly that many robotic walking battleships or this many gangly bombers. This game is like that. It comes off a bit tower defence-y often, kinda like Dungeon Defenders, where you have a mix of defenses and personal killingness. There's an extra gimmick, and it's a neat one I'll admit, where you can have multiple clones of yourself all doing different things at once. They call them "timelines" but think of them as preprogrammed clones. Send your clones out to do things, like attack a knot of monsters here, get a whack of resources there, set up a teleport beacon over yonder. Make use of that with subsequent clones. Between the various attack powers and the clones, various levels get solved by doing certain actions in a certain sequence, and it's up to you to figure out that sequence. They, and a lot of reviewers call it "puzzles", but it feels more like trial and error. Try a thing, have it fail, kinda like that RTS game. Try a slightly different thing, maybe it works. Build on that. And... I guess I didn't mind enough that I stayed up all night during my vacation time, playing this thing, but always with a lingering sense of resentment and frustration. There's a help menu option to get a hint on how to solve each given level, which I've found indispensible. It's a framework on which to build from. Marvellous. Oh, I'll finish the game, and I don't begrudge the purchase at all, but it's not quite as much a thing for me as I initially thought. It's a game for people with calm and composure. I'm a cussy weird uncle. Were it not for the hints, there'd be a lot more profanity in this review. You'd be seeing so many hearts you might mistake it for a loving letter to my wife. That aside, the character models are serviceable, but the lack of facial animation really gets to me. The protagonist looks kinda bug-eyed, like somebody cut pingpong balls in half and stuck them over her real eyes. She never blinks, ever. I know this is a petty thing, that for an indie game some facial animation is an expensive addition for little gameplay value, but it's still jarring to me. The game arenas are tightly controlled, with invisible barriers keeping you hemmed in. That's mostly fine, and 85% of the time it makes sense, but sometimes there's a barrier where the terrain looks open, and at least twice, there were no barriers when there should have been. It's not a show-stopper, but again... Ultimately, there was only one bug with the game, but it wasn't hard to work around it. It's been programmatically smooth otherwise. So I guess I like the coders, there's some indie pluck in this game. I'll be keeping my eye on them for whatever they make in the future, even if I'm not utterly swimmingly in love with this specific game. Something I forgot to add: It's actually nice seeing some Scots portrayed as Scots, as opposed to beardy li'l fatsos obsessed with runes and ale. That really needs mentioning. I mean, I'm not even Scottish, I'm just kind of embarrassed on their behalf when most of the time they're portrayed with a mug in one hand and an "oh aye laddy!" in the other, with nothing else at all to spare for them.

Just to take it off, I supported the game in kickstarter when I found one of the developers was in Sang Froid: Tales of Werewolves. The game works similar to this one, and other like Orcs Must Die. Like an action-RTS-tower defense hybrid, you can use magic to stop waves of enemies to reach certain places, creating traps or fighting the enemy yourself. The main attractive and what makes Timemelters different is the fact that you can go back in time and intervene again in the action, and again and again. It´s a wonderful mechanic, full of posibilities, which adds a lot to the fun of the game, too. The games looks beautiful, and the music is great. I miss a little more voiceover, but we could not reach the unlock in the campaign. About the difficulty, I find it pretty difficult in some stages, as I am so bad at multitasking... But nothing you cant go over just by trying. My only complain goes to the targeting system. for mee, feels a little stiff, and I find hard to aim. Maybe it´s due to my pc just reaching the bare minimum specs, or just my inability to aim, but it doesnt feel as smooth a I would like. But really, give the game try. Good news!

I had a lot of fun with this game! It's a mix between action, strategy and puzzles. All based on time travel. In missions, you have to choose which map's spot to target first, either to stop a dangerous enemy group or collect mana points you can spend on other spots. Here's the trick: you can go back in time to the start of the mission. Your past self will still perform the action you just did. If you have seen Back To The Furure II, that's excactly it. Your strategy must use the ability to use several versions of youself (one per timeline) to solve the puzzles. The action is challenging while not that hard, which is actually pretty nice. Puzzles are the great strengh of the game. Each puzzle is different so it never gets boring and game mechanics are introduced wisely. It's a very nice game, especially if you like solving puzzle with time.

A really clever, fun game. You run around casting spells and shooting enemies as they walk towards your base, but with the twist that you can rewind time. On the next time loop your past selves will still be on the map fighting, so you need to work around them to win. Killing some enemies gives you mana which lets you cast spells, so there is a strategy of getting mana on one loop, then resetting it and using it earlier in another loop to get more mana to power more spells etc. There are also some spells and mechanics which reset when you time loop, and some which don't, and playing around with this ends up becoming a big part of the puzzle. Overall a nice mix of a wave defense shooter and puzzle game. I would really recommend it, especially as a co-op game.

Really cool game that scratches the itch that Lemnis Gate has left me, using yourself as backup in a strategic way to complete particular objectives. One thing that stands out about the game is that every mission in the campaign has many unique ways to tackle it and the constant addition on new gameplay mechanics keeps the game feeling fresh. I had a lot of fun with the friend pass, the game has really good co-op. I'm excited for future expansions to the campaign.

This is honestly unbelievably good, the level of innovation and creative gameplay design reminds me of some of the best experimental outcomes from the PS2/Gamecube era of gaming. It's deeply fun and satisfying, and the way the game acclimatizes you to the 4D strategy is so seamless that you barely notice it happening until you're late in the game and suddenly you're coordinating a multilayered defensive strategy using 4 different timelines, not even knowing how you got to the point of being able to keep track of it all. This isn't the strongest story, nor the best voice acting, but it's 100% worth a try regardless because I haven't had this much fun with getting used to a mechanic since the first Portal. The one caveat to all of this is that at the end of the day this game feels like a proof of concept. The core mechanic is rock solid and perfectly implemented, but the limited number of spells don't allow for as varied a set of approaches. The maps are designed almost like puzzles with a specific correct solution, instead of as sandboxes that let you take any approach you want to a seemingly insurmountable challenge. I'd love to see something more along the lines of a system where you build a set of spells you have access to over the course of a campaign, letting you engage with the environment in a unique way based on your playstyle. Something like a 1 v 1 vs mode might be interesting to see as well. This is all the kind of thing I would hope to see as an evolution of the concept in a sequel, but for a first game breaking in a new idea, this is amazing.

The challenges helped me realise how dumb i was being in earlier maps. Loved it , will keep an eye out for DLC or their next project.

Timemelters is essentially a game where you co-operate with past versions of yourself (called 'echoes') by layering up timelines. And let me tell you, there's nothing cooler than crossing paths with an echo (or three) then later coming together and blasting a wave of enemies at just the right time. It's just incredibly satisfying to orchestrate. That's me! And that's me! That's also me! (Or... [i]was[/i] me?) https://youtu.be/FmbkJkXybuI Other games have explored this concept to some extent but in a strategy game with time and resource constraints as well as various abilities and cooldowns to juggle, pinch points against enemies and people to protect, it's just magic when it all comes together. Did you ever play the brilliant Sang-Froid - Tales of Werewolves? Well Timemelters is by some of the same developers and you can feel its cold blood coursing through this. Timemelters also deals with time distortion where later actions can interfere with past actions so this is a really clever game that takes some understanding. As such it does feel a little overwhelming at first. Everything is explained well and the interface does a great job of communicating a lot, it's just such a [i]different[/i] way to play a strategy game. That is, doing things now to facilitate things in the future. It's genuinely fascinating and so exciting once you get to grips with it. Speaking of which, Timemelters features oak yeet trees which curl their branches around enemies and just fling them. They're the best. Some folk have said Timemelters is like a puzzle game and while you'll spend a good while trying to work out ways of dealing with certain problems, the game is a lot more open than it initially seems. Some of the tighter scenarios or challenges have rigid solutions but the bigger ones with more moving parts allow for a fair bit of creativity. The story campaign is the meat of the experience and while it took me a while to get drawn into it, I eventually did and really enjoyed the ride. By the end I wanted more! Thankfully, Timemelters provides different difficulties (story, balanced, strategist), an 'extended' version of the story if you want more lore and depth, a co-op mode (with a free pass for a friend), a speedrun mode and 40+ challenges. It took me about 15-20 hours to complete the campaign on balanced/extended and now I can't wait for Tome II, or to play it with a friend. The thought of six or more echoes (yours [i]and[/i] theirs!) dashing about is dizzying... and very cool. Anyway, what a great, surprising and unique twist on real-time strategy, and all in third-person too.

The presentation and visuals of the game are probably the most lacking part of this experience, but the gameplay and puzzles feel to me like they're in *just* the right place between rewarding and nontrivial.

The main reason I'm giving this a thumbs down because this is not the complete game. Despite the title of the game being "Timemelters" on the Steam store page, when you boot up the game, the title on the menu is "Timemelters Tome 1 - Witches and Pyres". This game ends on a massively anticlimactic cliffhanger, which is always a huge negative since there's no guarantee said cliffhanger will ever get resolved. Also, if part 2 (or Tome 2) does come out, it's unknown if it'll be a free update to this game or a separate purchase. As for other other issues with the game, the Friend Pass version of this game doesn't work on Steam deck. I was playing through this with a friend of mine, and he tried to play the Friend Pass version on the Steam Deck, but we kept encountering a weird bug on the menu that kept him from doing anything. The full version of Timemelters works fine on Steam Deck. The game could have also done with a skip cutscene button. The story itself certainly fills space. Its not terrible, but neither is it anything new or interesting. I think the gameplay is unique, and it can be an enjoyable coop gaming experience (and I respect the devs for making it so that only 1 person has to buy the game). I just really wish this was the complete game and not just Part 1 (or for the Steam store page to make it very obvious that this is only Part 1).

I am enjoying this game, I am pretty anti-time travel but this game was great at walking me through the time mechanic. It doesn't hurt that tower defence is one of my favorite genres so this worked wonderfully.

Timemelters is an innovative blend of strategy, action, and puzzle genres that offers a unique and satisfying gameplay experience. The game revolves around a time-rewinding mechanic, allowing players to create "Echoes" of their past actions to help solve complex levels. This feature makes Timemelters a refreshing and engaging title, reminiscent of classic RTS games with a twist. The game's design encourages experimentation with multiple solutions to each level, enhancing replayability. Despite its linear map structure, the diverse objectives and mechanics keep the gameplay fresh and challenging. The co-op mode adds another layer of enjoyment, allowing friends to tackle the campaign together, even if only one person owns the game. While the graphics and character models may not be top-notch, the art style in the cutscenes is charming, and the soundtrack complements the game's atmosphere well. The story, involving witches and time travel, is captivating, though some players might find it less compelling than the gameplay itself. Timemelters does have a learning curve and minor kinks, but the developers appear to be responsive and committed to improvements. Overall, it's a standout indie title that combines creativity and strategic depth, making it a must-play for fans of puzzle and strategy games.

Timemelters is an inventive action–strategy hybrid that confidently builds its entire identity around the manipulation of time, offering an experience that feels both mechanically fresh and mentally demanding. Developed and published by Autoexec Games, the title blends real-time combat, tactical planning, and puzzle-like problem solving into a single cohesive loop, anchored by a narrative that gives emotional context to its systems rather than treating them as abstract mechanics. From the opening moments, the game establishes a world on the brink of collapse and positions the player as an unlikely hero whose greatest weapon is not raw power, but the ability to learn from failure and literally rewind it. The story follows Teagan, a young woman accused of witchcraft and saved from execution by a mysterious temporal force. What begins as a personal escape quickly escalates into a high-stakes struggle to prevent an apocalyptic future. The narrative is delivered through a mix of dialogue, environmental storytelling, and optional lore, allowing players to engage as deeply as they choose without overwhelming the pacing. This flexible approach to storytelling complements the gameplay well, ensuring that narrative moments enhance rather than interrupt the constant cycle of experimentation and strategy. At the heart of Timemelters lies its defining mechanic: time rewinding that creates echoes of your past actions. Instead of simply undoing mistakes, rewinding time spawns deterministic versions of Teagan that repeat exactly what you previously did. These echoes fight alongside your present self, effectively allowing you to coordinate with your own past decisions. This system transforms combat encounters into layered tactical challenges, where success often depends on planning several timelines ahead rather than reacting in the moment. It is a mechanic that feels immediately novel but grows increasingly deep as the game introduces more complex scenarios and enemy behaviors. Combat itself strikes a careful balance between urgency and fragility. Teagan is extremely vulnerable, often falling in a single hit, which creates constant tension and discourages reckless play. To compensate, she has access to a variety of magical abilities, environmental tools, and summoned allies that can be deployed strategically across timelines. Every encounter becomes a puzzle of positioning, timing, and foresight, where knowing when to rewind is just as important as knowing when to advance. When a plan finally comes together—past echoes drawing enemy fire while the present Teagan executes the final move—the sense of payoff is substantial. Level design plays a crucial role in reinforcing this loop. Missions vary in structure, ranging from defensive stand-offs and escort objectives to boss encounters that demand precise coordination across multiple timelines. The inclusion of a tactical pause and overhead planning view allows players to reassess the battlefield and adjust their approach, which is essential given how quickly situations can spiral out of control. While some scenarios lean toward trial-and-error, these moments rarely feel unfair; instead, they encourage experimentation and reinforce the game’s core philosophy of learning through repetition. Visually, Timemelters presents a stylized fantasy world that prioritizes clarity over spectacle. Character models and environments may not rival larger-budget productions, but they serve the gameplay effectively, keeping enemy movements and spell effects readable even during chaotic encounters. The audio design supports the atmosphere with restrained but effective music and sound cues that heighten tension without becoming distracting. Together, these elements create a presentation that feels purposeful, even if it occasionally shows its indie roots. One of the game’s most welcome features is its cooperative mode, which allows the entire campaign to be played with another player. In co-op, the already complex time mechanics gain an additional layer of depth, as coordination between two players must now account for multiple timelines and overlapping strategies. Communication becomes essential, and successful execution feels even more rewarding when achieved through teamwork rather than solo planning. This mode significantly enhances replayability and offers a different perspective on challenges that may feel overwhelming alone. Beyond the main campaign, Timemelters includes additional modes such as challenges and speedrun-focused content, extending its longevity for players who wish to fully master its systems. These modes emphasize efficiency, precision, and creative use of time manipulation, reinforcing the game’s strengths and rewarding deep understanding of its mechanics. Ultimately, Timemelters stands out as a thoughtfully designed title that dares to demand patience, planning, and persistence from its players. While its learning curve and occasional difficulty spikes may not appeal to everyone, those willing to engage with its systems will find a uniquely satisfying experience that turns failure into progress and time itself into a tactical resource. It is a game that proves originality does not require excess, only a clear vision and the confidence to fully commit to it. Rating: 8/10

Not quite for me but i'm still glad unique indie games like this exist. This is a tower defense game with a time loop mechanic where you create loops of yourself called an "echo" that will repeat your previous actions. So rather than having the typical TD gameplay loop of "build weak towers in first waves, upgrade to better ones in later waves", it's better to treat this game more like a puzzler that uses Tower defense as the mechanic. Your attacks are slow and you don't cleave through massive amounts of enemies with your "towers". that's not what this game is. It's slow and methodical, you need to literally plan ahead for your final timeline and set up a winning path on each mission. Obviously with my in-game time I didn't finish the game. Most of my reasons why are preferential, not critical. I'm writing this review to encourage people to try this and support indie that are willing to give us unique and interesting mechanics rather than dopamine/grind slop. This may be your thing, and it goes on sale quite often too.
